subject: blister beetle
title: Hundreds of Beetle Larvae Pile Up to Impersonate One Female Bee

scenes.text: That bee on the stem isn't a bee.
It's a clump of blister beetle larvae. Hundreds of them, each two millimeters long.
Together they match a female digger bee in size and color, and copy her scent.
A male bee flies in to mate. Within two seconds, the whole clump is clinging to him.
When he meets a real female, they switch to her. She flies them to her nest.
There they eat her pollen, her nectar and her egg. The fake bee was a way in.

description:
In California's Mojave Desert, newly hatched larvae of the blister beetle Meloe franciscanus climb a plant stem and bunch into a clump of 120 to more than 2,000 that looks like a female digger bee.
The clump also gives off a chemical that mimics her sex pheromone. A male bee tries to mate with it and the whole mass transfers to him within 0.13 to 2 seconds; when he reaches a real female the larvae move to her, ride to her nest and feed on the pollen, the nectar and the bee's egg (PNAS, 2006).
Smartest trick a parasite has ever pulled? Comment below.
thumbnail_text: THAT BEE IS A PILE OF BEETLES
first_comment: One female beetle lays an average of 761 eggs, and the larvae move up and down the stem as a single unit. Would the fake bee have fooled you?
